Four days after these strange events, a funeral procession left Canterville Chase at about eleven at night. Eight black horses pulled the hearse, each wearing a large tuft of swaying ostrich feathers on its head. A rich purple cloth covered the lead coffin, with the Canterville coat of arms embroidered on it in gold. Servants carrying burning torches walked beside the hearse and the carriages, making the whole procession wonderfully impressive. Lord Canterville, who had travelled from Wales especially for the funeral, was the chief mourner. He rode in the first carriage with little Virginia. The United States Minister and his wife followed, then Washington and the three boys, with Mrs. Umney in the last carriage. Everyone felt that, after being frightened by the ghost for more than fifty years, she deserved to see him finally laid to rest. A deep grave had been dug in a corner of the churchyard beneath the old yew tree, and the Reverend Augustus Dampier read the service with great solemnity. After the ceremony, the servants put out their torches, following an old Canterville family custom. As the coffin was lowered into the grave, Virginia stepped forward and placed a large cross of white and pink almond blossoms on it. At that moment the moon emerged from behind a cloud and silently filled the little churchyard with silver light. A nightingale began singing in a distant patch of woodland. Virginia remembered the ghost’s description of the Garden of Death. Tears blurred her eyes, and she barely spoke on the journey home.

The next morning, before Lord Canterville left for London, Mr. Otis spoke with him about the jewels the ghost had given Virginia. They were magnificent, particularly a ruby necklace in an old Venetian setting, a superb piece of sixteenth-century craftsmanship. They were so valuable that Mr. Otis had serious doubts about allowing his daughter to accept them.

‘My lord,’ he said, ‘I understand that in this country the law of mortmain, concerning property held permanently, applies to jewellery as well as land. It seems perfectly clear that these jewels are, or ought to be, your family heirlooms. I therefore ask you to take them to London with you. Please consider them simply a part of your property that has returned to you in rather unusual circumstances. As for my daughter, she is still only a child and, I am happy to say, so far takes very little interest in these ornaments of idle luxury.’

You must adopt a little of my philosophy. Remember the past only when remembering it gives you pleasure.”

“I cannot give you credit for any such philosophy. Your memories must be so entirely free of anything to regret that the satisfaction they bring comes from something better than philosophy: innocence. With me, it is different. Painful memories force themselves upon me, and I cannot—and should not—push them away. All my life I have been selfish in my actions, though not in my principles. As a child, I learned what was right, but nobody taught me to control my temper. I was given good principles and then allowed to follow them with pride and conceit. Unfortunately, as an only son—and for many years an only child—I was spoiled by my parents. Though they were good people themselves, especially my father, who was kind and generous in every way, they allowed, encouraged, almost taught me to be selfish and overbearing. I cared for nobody beyond my family and thought poorly of everyone else, or at least wanted to think their intelligence and worth inferior to mine. That was how I lived from eight to twenty-eight, and might still be living but for you, my dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! How much I owe you! You taught me a lesson that was painful at first, but immensely valuable. You humbled me as I deserved. I approached you without the slightest doubt that I would be accepted. You showed me how little all my advantages could do to win a woman worth winning.”

“Had you really convinced yourself that I would accept?”

“I had indeed. What must you think of my vanity? I believed you wanted and expected me to propose.”

“Then my manner must have been misleading, though I assure you it was unintentional. I never meant to deceive you, but my high spirits may often have led me astray. How you must have hated me after that evening!”

“Hated you! Perhaps I was angry at first, but my anger soon began to turn in the right direction.”

“I am almost afraid to ask what you thought when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“No, truly. I felt only surprise.”

“You cannot have been more surprised than I was by your acknowledging me. My conscience told me I deserved no special kindness, and I admit I did not expect more than I deserved.”

“My purpose then,” Darcy replied, “was to show you every courtesy I could, so you would see that I was not petty enough to resent the past. I hoped to earn your forgiveness and improve your opinion of me by showing you that I had taken your criticisms to heart.

The next morning she was discovered dead in bed, apparently without having experienced any pain. Sir Mathew Reid was summoned immediately, though naturally nothing could be done, and her burial at Beauchamp Chalcote was arranged for the 22nd. A few days before her death she had drawn up her will, bequeathing to Lord Arthur her small Curzon Street house, together with her furniture, personal belongings, and pictures. The exceptions were her miniatures, destined for her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and an amethyst necklace, which was left to Sybil Merton. The estate was not worth a great deal, but Mr. Mansfield, her solicitor, was most anxious that Lord Arthur should return immediately if he could, since numerous bills required payment and Lady Clementina had never maintained proper accounts.

Lady Clementina’s kindly remembrance moved Lord Arthur deeply, and he thought that Mr. Podgers had much to answer for. Nevertheless, his love for Sybil outweighed every other feeling, while the knowledge of having performed his duty brought him comfort and peace. By the time he reached Charing Cross, he was entirely happy.

The Mertons welcomed him with great kindness. Sybil required him to promise that he would never again let anything separate them, and June 7th was chosen for the wedding. Life appeared bright and lovely to him once more, and all his former happiness returned.

One day, however, while he was sorting through the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil, burning bundles of faded correspondence and emptying drawers of miscellaneous rubbish, the girl suddenly uttered a small delighted cry.

‘What is it you have found, Sybil?’ Lord Arthur asked, looking up from his task with a smile.

‘This beautiful little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. Isn’t it delightfully quaint and Dutch? Please let me have it! I am certain amethysts will not suit me until I am past eighty.’

It was the little box that had contained the aconitine.

Lord Arthur gave a start, and a slight flush rose to his cheek. What he had done had almost completely slipped his mind. He thought it a strange coincidence that Sybil, for whose sake he had endured all that dreadful anxiety, should be the first person to recall it to him.

‘Certainly you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.’

‘Oh, thank you, Arthur! And may I have the bonbon as well? I never imagined Lady Clementina enjoyed sweets. I supposed her much too intellectual.’

Lord Arthur turned deathly pale, and a dreadful thought passed through his mind.
